newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rivals plot in wings in Yeltsin's absence.
newsitem.headline: Rivals plot in wings in Yeltsin's absence.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin's latest illness has revived power struggles unleashed by his health problems in mid-1996, but many rivals are now playing a more stealthy waiting game.

When Yeltsin was laid low by heart problems just before he was re-elected last July, the Kremlin was unable to conceal the fierce jostling for power that ensued among leaders who believed the president would not return to power.

This time, with Yeltsin ill with pneumonia, the manoeuvring behind the scenes has caused less of a sensation in the Russian and Western media and much of the plotting remains behind the scenes. But the protaganists and the stakes remain the same.
"Everyone understands now that you must not fight in the open but negotiate in the wings," political analyst Lilia Shevtsova told Reuters.

"There are several rival groups preparing for the decisive moment when Yeltsin leaves the political scene, and that could come at any moment. They are trying to strengthen their position now and in preparation for when Yeltsin goes."
The likely presidential candidates remain the same as last summer and autumn, when infighting reached a peak before Yeltsin sacked his ambitious security adviser, Alexander Lebed.

They are Lebed, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, communist leader Gennady Zyuganov and Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov. Influential figures behind the scenes are Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais and powerful financial groups.
The infighting is less ferocious than last autumn, largely because Lebed has been ousted, but there is no doubt that even Yeltsin's allies are focusing on the question of his successor.
The president is isolated at a residence outside Moscow from which he travels occasionally to the Kremlin. Doctors say he needs at least 10 days to two weeks more to recover fully.
Television footage of a thin and sometimes glazed-looking Yeltsin fail to end doubts about his ability to rule at the age of 66 after at least two heart attacks and major heart surgery.
The aim of those around the president is to hold on to the power they have through him. Simliar concerns drive financial groups which have an interest in continuity.

"It's a matter of consolidating the basic part of the ruling circles around the candidacy of a successor to the president, a successor whom the (ruling) elite consider acceptable to themselves," the liberal newspaper Nezavisimaya Gazeta said.

"The Russian ruling elites on the whole need stability. Moreover, they have been without a 'boss' for quite a long time -- more than six months -- and have got a taste for indepedent decision-making."
Many political pundits would expect Lebed, 46, to win a new election if it were held soon. But he is despised or mistrusted by leaders across the political spectrum.
Much plotting under way now is shaped by a fear of the unpredictable and tough-talking Lebed coming to power, and this idea unites politicians who agree on little or nothing else.

Chernomyrdin, 58, has been a loyal ally to Yeltsin and would be likely to continue reforms. But his dour image and the unpopular economic reforms he has presided over could make him unelectable, even with the state machinery behind him.

Luzkhov, 60, has also backed Yeltsin and reforms. He appears to have been campaigning unofficially by travelling outside Moscow and commenting on issues outside his domain, but his short-term chances of victory look slim.
Zyuganov, 52, has demanded that Yeltsin be ousted for health reasons, but many analysts say he does not believe he can win an election and doubt he is commited to a new poll.
For these reasons, much of the talk in the wings is of political alliances and constitutional amendments that would prevent Lebed coming to power.

These include allowing Chernomyrdin to serve as president until the end of Yeltsin's scheduled term if Yeltsin dies, reducing the president's vast powers, setting up a state council to govern or having the president chosen by parliament.
"The problem is that no single idea is acceptable to all political groups, which means an election could go ahead if Yeltsin left the political scene," Shevtsova said.
"Much will depend on whether a political consensus can be reached in the coming months."
